newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain sees EMU as path to greater role.
newsitem.headline: Spain sees EMU as path to greater role.

text.p: For Spain, participation in Europe's single currency fulfils its need to belong, to be accepted and to assume its rightful place at Europe's core after years at the edge under a fascist dictator and the fragile democracy that followed.
Few Spaniards have grumbled at the austerity policies adopted to ensure Spain is fit for the launch, because the economic merits or drawbacks of the plan are of only secondary importance to them.
They are inspired, instead, by a new international vision of Spain's role after decades focused on domestic politics.

"Spain wants to be taken seriously by its partners," said a Western diplomat. "Spain is one of the five largest EU countries and wants out of its fringe position. It can claim this role only if it is in European Monetary Union from the beginning." WIDE ACCEPTANCE OF EMU DRIVE
Despite high unemployment and government belt-tightening, public acceptance of the plan has been high, and future economic problems are unlikely to shake this commitment.

"There is no group that does not profess its European faith, that does not organise interminable congresses and forums about the European future and its effects," wrote local financial daily La Gaceta de los Negocios.

The conservative Popular Party government, which took over in May after 13 years of socialist rule, adopted its predecessors' European economic policy with little fuss and set about revitalising the drive to whip finances into shape.

King Juan Carlos, who rarely steps into national politics, told the country this year it was essential to be in the single currency, effectively clipping the wings of any political party which might have considered turning EMU into an issue.
Among Spain's major political parties, only the communist-led United Left opposes the nation's European goal, calling it a plot evolved by European elites solely for their own benefit.

"In Spain there is a broad consensus between the opposition and the government over the need for convergence, so (Prime Minister Jose Maria) Aznar made the (socialists') 1994 ...declaration on convergence his own," the diplomat said.
The government has put the public mood to the test, presenting a tough budget for 1997 -- the crucial year for the measurement of economic fitness for the single currency.
It slashed the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, as required, from 6.6 percent in 1995, thanks to above-average revenue growth and severe cuts in spending.
The unusual thriftiness has prompted cost-cutting by ministries and other public bodies.
The government froze public sector pay to cut spending growth, triggering a protest demonstration of some 200,000 people in Madrid last month.
But there has been almost no resonance in society at large -- a salary freeze for public employees is unlikely to strike a chord when 20 percent of the potential workforce is unemployed.
Spain has the highest unemployment rate in Europe. DRAMATIC PROGRESS TO MEET CRITERIA
The government has launched an aggressive campaign to press unions and businesses towards a consensus pact to crack open Spain's labour market and foster job creation.
To enter the currency union at its expected launch in 1999, Spain must also meet criteria on public debt, long-term interest rates, inflation and exchange-rate stability.
Much of the dramatic improvement in these criteria, together with growth above the European average, may well have helped Spaniards come to terms with the upcoming changes.
Inflation has declined steadily. The peseta has stabilised and held firm after its most recent devaluation in spring 1995.

Most dramatically, the difference in yield between Spanish bonds and their sturdier German counterparts has narrowed sharply, suggesting that the extra risks involved in holding Spanish debt no longer warrant a great premium.
The spread had shrunk to 129 basis points on November 27 from 330 at the start of March, and from 500 in mid-1995.

And if Spanish bonds look a bit more like German bonds, no Spaniard is going to lose any sleep if the peseta starts to look more like the mark or disappears altogether, replaced by the planned single currency.
There are no signs of fears in Spain like those that worry Germans who fret about instability if they lose their currency.
Nor would the peseta's demise signify the death of a major international currency, such as sterling, with its memories of Britain's old imperial grandeur.
For Spain, the bid to regain a bit of its past glory is well worth any temporary economic inconvenience.
The fledgling government, backed by this strong national consensus, has already begun to flex its political muscle.
Spain has sought a role among European leaders in NATO and was the first to heed calls to help in strife-torn Zaire, offering troops to help keep the peace.

It has also raised its hand in an area of traditional foreign policy ties, Latin America, and ended up with a diplomatic crisis on its hands for pushing the European Union into a harder line against Communist leader Fidel Castro.

"Spain is right in thinking that the new integrative identity of the EU is not a fixed characteristic, but a dynamic process. Spain must be a part of this dynamic if it doesn't want to fall by the wayside," the diplomat said.
